name: Graphic Designer
intro: A graphic designer's résumé works alongside a portfolio, so its job is to give context: what kinds of work you do, for whom, with which tools, and what happened after the work went out. Keep the layout clean and readable; it is itself a sample of your typography.
recruiterFocus: A portfolio link near the top, with work that matches the job: brand, packaging, editorial, digital or motion.
The type of clients or employers you have designed for, and the media you produce (print, signage, social, packaging).
Tool fluency, mainly Adobe Illustrator, InDesign and Photoshop, plus Figma or motion tools where relevant.
Print production know-how: file preparation, colour management, finishes and working with printers.
Evidence that the work met a business goal, such as sales, sign-ups, or a successful launch.
experienceTips: Describe the projects, not just the role: 'identity systems for 11 clients' beats 'created designs for clients'.
Name the outcome where you know it: sales after a rebrand, entries after a campaign, fewer reprints after a new checklist.
Show ownership: guidelines you wrote, templates you built, juniors you reviewed.
Mention collaboration with copywriters, photographers, printers and developers.
Link each major project to a portfolio case study if you can.
numbersTips: Output: 'designed 40 print jobs a month', '20-title book series', '240-product packaging range'.
Results: 'season ticket sales up 14% after the rebrand' or 'online gift-card sales up 19% year over year'.
Efficiency: 'templates cut layout time from a day to three hours' or 'reprints reduced from 8% of jobs to 2%'.
Scale and budget: 'managed a $650,000 production budget' or 'rolled out signage across nine shops'.
noExperience: Lead with your portfolio and your best two or three student or personal projects, with a short brief and result for each.
Count placements, freelance jobs, student societies, local events and volunteer work for charities.
List design competitions, exhibitions or student shows you were selected for.
Keep the résumé to one page and let the portfolio carry the detail.
hardSkills: Accessible design for print and digital

softSkills.proof: Mention client presentations and how quickly you turned around revision rounds.
Show a process you set up to catch errors, like a pre-flight checklist, and the drop in reprints.
Name the people you worked with, such as copywriters, printers, photographers or developers, on a specific project.
Give your typical volume or a deadline you hit, like a campaign delivered for a launch date.
For mid and senior roles, say how many juniors you reviewed or coached and how.

education: Most roles ask for a degree or diploma in graphic or communication design, but a strong portfolio can outweigh formal education. Common qualifications include a US B.F.A., a UK BA (Hons), a Canadian college diploma or Québec DEC, an Australian TAFE Diploma of Graphic Design, a German B.A. in Kommunikationsdesign, or an Indian B.Des or BFA in Applied Art.

certifications.name: Adobe Certified Professional
certifications.note: Can help entry-level designers show tool skills, though a portfolio usually matters more.

certifications.name: Short courses in motion, accessibility or packaging
certifications.note: Worth listing if the job asks for those specialisms.

certifications.name: Professional body membership (e.g. AIGA, RGD, DIA, AGDA)
certifications.note: Shows engagement with the profession; RGD in Ontario also offers a 'Registered Graphic Designer' designation.

summaryExample: Graphic designer with six years in brand and packaging design for food and retail clients. Take projects from concept to press, write brand guidelines and manage printers. A packaging refresh for a coffee range led to a 12% rise in supermarket sales.
objectiveExample: Graphic design graduate seeking a junior designer role in a branding studio. Strong in Illustrator and InDesign, with placement experience in signage and print, and a portfolio covering identity, packaging and editorial projects.
summaryVsObjective: Use a summary once you have professional design work to point to: specialism, sectors and one result. Use an objective if you are a graduate or changing careers, and direct the reader to the portfolio projects that best show your potential.
extraSections: Portfolio link (and a Behance or Dribbble profile if it is up to date).
Awards, exhibitions and shortlists, with the year.
Selected clients, if you are allowed to name them.
Teaching, workshops or talks you have given.

weakStrong.strong: Created identity systems for 11 clients, from logo and colour palette to signage and stationery.
weakStrong.why: It shows breadth, volume and the full scope of the work.

weakStrong.strong: Led the rebrand of a 400-seat theatre; season ticket sales rose 14% in the first year.
weakStrong.why: It shows ownership and a business result linked to the design.

weakStrong.strong: Introduced a two-step proof sign-off that cut printer-rejected artwork from 8% of jobs to under 2%.
weakStrong.why: It turns a routine task into a measurable quality improvement.

takeaways: Put a portfolio link at the top and make sure it opens.
Describe projects and outcomes, not just duties.
Show print and production knowledge alongside creative skills.
Keep the layout clean: your résumé is a design sample.
Tailor the work and skills to the job's specialism.

countryNotes.us: No licence is needed. A B.F.A. or B.A. in graphic design is common, and a portfolio is expected with every application. Use US Letter size for a PDF résumé and leave out photos.
countryNotes.uk: No licence is needed. A BA (Hons) in graphic design or a related subject is common, and job levels are often called junior, mid-weight and senior. Call it a CV and attach or link a portfolio.
countryNotes.ca: No licence is needed, though the RGD in Ontario offers a 'Registered Graphic Designer' designation. Packaging and labels sold in Canada generally need English and French text, and Québec has extra French-language rules, so bilingual layout experience is useful.
countryNotes.au: No licence is needed. A TAFE Diploma of Graphic Design or a Bachelor of Design are common routes. Check the job ad for software needs, and attach a portfolio link. Australian spelling (colour, organise) applies.
countryNotes.de: No licence is needed. Typical qualifications are a B.A. in Kommunikationsdesign or an Ausbildung as Mediengestalter/in Digital und Print. Accessibility rules (BFSG) increasingly apply to digital products, so accessible PDF or web experience is worth mentioning. Give language levels in CEFR.
countryNotes.in: No licence is needed. Common qualifications include a B.Des, a BFA in Applied Art or a diploma in design. Agency titles such as Visualiser and Art Director are widely used. For packaging, knowledge of FSSAI and Legal Metrology label requirements is a plus.
